edits.html:
Foot Puncture Wound Infection

Red, tender foot weeks after a nail through a shoe · NBME · what exposure did the stem give?

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo M seen 3 weeks after a nail went through his shoe into the right sole; the wound was cleaned and dressed, but moderate pain persists; last tetanus vaccine at age 5, otherwise healthy; T 37.2 C, other vitals normal; the site is red, warm and tender · Q — the most likely causal organism; options spanned Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, group A streptococcus, Aeromonas hydrophila and Klebsiella pneumoniae
The decision point

A foot that stays painful, red, warm and tender weeks after a nail went through a shoe suggests osteomyelitis from direct inoculation. The classic organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It colonizes the foam inner sole of athletic shoes, and the nail carries it into bone or cartilage. Systemic signs are often minimal; this boy's temperature was 37.2 C.

Infection in the first few days after a puncture is usually cellulitis from Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci. S. aureus is also the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall. Pseudomonas is the classic organism only for the delayed bone or cartilage infection after a puncture through a shoe.

Wound organisms by exposurewhat the history must supply for each
OrganismExposure and courseKey discriminatorWhy less likely here
Pseudomonas aeruginosaNail through the sole of an athletic shoe; pain, redness and tenderness persist or return days to weeks laterPuncture through a shoe with a delayed deep infectionFits: shoe puncture and a 3-week course
Staphylococcus aureusMost common cause of osteomyelitis overall, by blood spread or direct inoculation; most common cause of early infection after a punctureEarly cellulitis or abscess, or osteomyelitis without a shoe punctureThe puncture through a shoe makes Pseudomonas more likely
Aeromonas hydrophilaWound contaminated by fresh water at the time of injury; also diarrhea and infections in immunocompromised hostsFreshwater exposure at injuryNo water exposure
Group A streptococcusPharyngitis, impetigo, erysipelas and cellulitis; necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shockFast-spreading superficial skin infectionNot the classic cause of a delayed bone infection after a puncture
Klebsiella pneumoniaeAspiration pneumonia, for example in alcohol use disorderLung infection with an aspiration riskNo lung source and no link to puncture wounds
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Plain radiograph of the footFirstOften normal early; may show a retained radiopaque foreign bodyA normal film does not exclude osteomyelitis
MRI of the footNextMarrow edemaOsteomyelitis; more sensitive than radiographs
Bone culture at surgical debridementConfirmsOrganism grownNames the organism and guides antibiotics
Scenario bank
Management Osteomyelitis after a puncture needs surgical debridement to remove dead tissue. Bone cultures taken at debridement name the organism. Empiric antibiotics should cover both Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus until cultures return.
Decoy note The tetanus history does not point to any organism. His last dose was 2 years earlier, within the 5-year limit for a puncture wound, so he needs no booster. A near-normal temperature does not argue against bone infection after a puncture.
Pearls Pseudomonas is a gram-negative rod that is aerobic and oxidase-positive · Aeromonas hydrophila infects wounds exposed to fresh water; Vibrio vulnificus infects wounds exposed to salt water · How NBME framed it: the stem never names osteomyelitis, and the options set the key beside S. aureus and a water-borne organism.
Pairs with Part I Septic Arthritis of the Hip lists joint organisms by host. Pyelonephritis: Naming the Organism keys Pseudomonas for a catheter-associated urinary infection. Ask which the stem supplies: a host, a site or an exposure.
Transferable rule Name the organism from the exposure in the history. A delayed deep foot infection after a nail through a shoe points to Pseudomonas. Without that exposure, S. aureus remains the most common cause of osteomyelitis.
Unchecked attributeStaphylococcus aureus — the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall, but a nail through a shoe with a delayed bone infection points to Pseudomonas.
True-fact-wrong-slotAeromonas hydrophila — a real wound pathogen, but it needs fresh-water exposure at the time of injury, which this boy did not have.
True-fact-wrong-slotGroup A streptococcus — causes pharyngitis and fast-spreading skin infections, not the classic delayed bone infection after a puncture.
Class-vs-memberKlebsiella pneumoniae — a gram-negative rod like the key, but it causes pneumonia in patients prone to aspiration, not puncture-wound osteomyelitis.
